olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: Each of eight boxes contains six balls. Each ball has one of $n$ colors; no two balls in the same box share a color; no two colors appear together in more than one box. Find the smallest $n$ for which this is possible.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 2001

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: $\triangle ABC$ with incircle $\omega$ tangent to $BC,AC$ at $D_1,E_1$. $D_2\in BC$, $E_2\in AC$ with $CD_2=BD_1$ and $CE_2=AE_1$. $P=AD_2\cap BE_2$; $Q$ = closer intersection of $\omega$ with $AD_2$ to $A$. Prove $AQ=D_2P$.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 2001

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: Let $P$ be a point such that $PA,PB,PC$ are sides of an obtuse triangle, with the obtuse angle opposing $PA$. Prove $\angle BAC$ is acute.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 2001

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: Let $S$ be a set of integers with (a) $\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(a-2,b-2)=1$ for some $a,b\in S$; (b) if $x,y\in S$, then $x^2-y\in S$. Prove $S=\mathbb{Z}$.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 2001

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: Each point in the plane is assigned a real number so that for any triangle, the number at the incenter equals the arithmetic mean of the three vertex numbers. Prove all points have the same number.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 2001
